source.title: Learning from Emergence: A Study on Proactively Inhibiting the Monosemantic Neurons of Artificial Neural Networks
source.authors: Jia-Chuan Wang; Shimin Di; Lei Chen; Charles Wang Wai Ng

record.tranche_reason: The study measures a monosemanticity metric and tests an intervention intended to reduce it, but it does not test whether neurons respond to unrelated input features or any listed claim version.
record.gate_note: Table 4 directly reports changes in the study's Monosemantic Scale metric under different intervention conditions. These results are recorded as related findings, not evidence for a listed version. Tables 1–3 and 5–9 report downstream task performance and comparisons, not measurements of neuronal semantics; cited findings are not recorded as rows.
record.test_reason: The study never measures whether neurons respond to unrelated features. Its Monosemantic Scale is a per-neuron activation-deviation score, (z−mean)²/variance, which needs no feature set. It uses this score to drive a training intervention (Reverse Deactivation) and reports downstream task scores. Table 4 shows only small changes in that score, which is a related but different construct from polysemanticity. The Pythia figures (Figs 1–2) are illustrations with no prevalence rates.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors also hypothesize that fewer monosemantic neurons is a key driver of performance gains with scale. They conclude Reverse Deactivation inhibits monosemanticity on their metric, and that MEmeL matches or slightly improves BERT, Swin and ConvGRU results (p ≤ 0.07). They concede the Table 4 decrease is small and attribute this to the learning rate.
record.recipe_differences: The study proposes an online Monosemantic Scale metric and Reverse Deactivation training intervention; it does not apply the original sources' neuron-feature analysis to test mixed responses.
record.method_sensitivity: The measured decrease ratio varies with the inhibition method: it is positive for Original and Reverse Deactivation, and negative for both naive methods.

fits_no_version.finding: On Swin-B, with 10k neuron samples, Reverse Deactivation gave a 0.013% average decrease in the authors' Monosemantic Scale, against 0.003% for no modification. Both naive deactivation methods gave negative decrease ratios (−0.017%, −0.044%).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: A gradient-reversing deactivation slightly lowers an online activation-outlier score, while naive deactivation raises it.

fits_no_version.finding: Fig. 2: deactivating a probe-identified 'French' neuron in Pythia-v0 raises loss on French inputs less in larger models (70M vs 1B vs 6.9B). This is shown in a figure only, with no numbers in the text.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Single-feature neurons matter less to loss as language-model scale grows.

record.peer_reviewed: Proceedings of the 30th ACM SIGKDD Conference on Knowledge Discovery and Data Mining (KDD '24)
record.problems: The neuron-semantic result is reported for Swin-B only, as averages over 10k neuron samples; Table 4 gives no uncertainty estimates. The paper describes the Reverse Deactivation decrease ratio as relatively small. Its metric does not directly establish that neurons respond to unrelated features.
record.rows_left_out: Downstream task scores in Tables 1–3 and 5–9 are not direct measurements of neuron semantics and were not included as rows.

untested.parts: No analysis of image-classifier neurons responding to unrelated inputs. Swin-B is used only for the Monosemantic Scale and accuracy.
No prevalence or layer distribution of polysemantic MLP neurons in language models. Pythia appears only in illustrative figures.
Superposition as cause is not tested. The capacity story appears only as an analogy (Appendix A).
No share of polysemantic neurons is measured across architectures or regularizers. The intervention aims to raise, not lower, polysemanticity, and is scored with a non-feature metric.
Not tested, though the paper notes there is no consensus definition of activation or monosemanticity.

record.verdict_notes: The Monosemantic Scale measures how far a neuron's activation deviates from its running mean. It never checks which features the neuron responds to, so it cannot establish mono- versus polysemanticity in the claim's sense. The paper cites both original sources (Zoom In, SoLU) only as background.

versions.untested_parts: Whether image-classifier neurons respond to several unrelated inputs.
The prevalence and layer-wise distribution of neurons responding to unrelated tokens or contexts in language models.
Whether polysemanticity is caused by sparse features being packed under capacity pressure.
Whether polysemanticity arises without capacity pressure from initialization, regularization, or training noise.
Whether the share of polysemantic neurons varies with activation function, architecture, or regularization, and whether that share can be lowered without a large performance loss.
Whether apparent mixed neuron responses resolve into a shared feature or related jobs with better interpretability tools.
Whether polysemanticity judgments depend on activation range or explanation scoring.
